purpose: Imipramine is mainly used to treat depression, but doctors also prescribe it for bedwetting in children and sometimes for anxiety or panic disorder. It can help improve your mood, sleep, energy, and overall sense of well-being. In children, it helps the bladder hold urine better through the night.
how_it_works: Your brain uses chemical messengers called serotonin and norepinephrine to help regulate your mood and emotions. Imipramine works by preventing your brain from reabsorbing these chemicals too quickly, so they stay active longer and help improve how you feel. Think of it like keeping more of the good chemicals available for your brain to use.
common_side_effects: Dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, feeling dizzy or lightheaded when you stand up, drowsiness, weight gain, difficulty urinating, and increased sweating. These are often most noticeable when you first start the medication and may improve over time.
warnings: Do not stop taking this medication suddenly without talking to your doctor, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms. Imipramine can cause serious heart rhythm changes, so tell your doctor if you have any heart problems. It may increase suicidal thoughts in children, teenagers, and young adults, especially early in treatment — contact your doctor right away if this happens. Avoid alcohol while taking this medication. Do not take it if you have recently taken an MAO inhibitor, as this combination can be very dangerous.
typical_dosing: For adults with depression, the usual starting dose is 75 mg per day, often split into smaller doses, and this may be gradually increased up to 200 mg per day or sometimes higher under close medical supervision. For children with bedwetting, doses are typically much lower, usually 25 mg taken about one hour before bedtime. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose.
